title: PZK versus SZK
formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that on \(x\in Y\) the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(1- \varepsilon (|x|)\), and on \(x\in N\) every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most \(\varepsilon (|x|)\). Negligible means smaller than |\(x|^{- d}\) for every fixed \(d>0\) at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside \(Y\cup N\). The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of \((\mathrm{P},V*)(x)\), for every \(x\in Y\). Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

why: Determine whether allowing any negligible statistical simulation error increases the expressive power of information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between two information-theoretic privacy notions, posed in a standard cryptography textbook, supported by a nontrivial oracle separation and explicitly retained in recent work on perfect zero knowledge.

progress.text: Goldreich lists PZK versus SZK as open and distinguishes strict from expected-time simulation.
The journal paper proves an oracle separation of SZK from PZK, not an ordinary class separation.
The PCP paper explicitly retains the ordinary interactive-proof equality as unknown.

status_note: No unrelativized resolution was found through 11 September 2026. The 2024 paper explicitly retains the equality as open. Oracle separations and perfect-zero-knowledge results in PCP or multiprover models do not settle this target.
review_note: Reviewed using the corrected PZK definition in ECCC TR16-140 revision 3, including the allowed failure symbol. The promise-problem convention follows that paper; the textbook motivates the underlying class comparison. No duplicate was found, including streaming record TCS-1929.
